newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-U.S. grandmaster takes unexpected route to dream.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.S. grandmaster takes unexpected route to dream.

text.p: Joel Benjamin dreamed about playing the world chess champion one day but he never imagined it would be quite like this.

The American grandmaster was hired by IBM to help programme the chess-playing supercomputer Deep Blue for its re-match next month with Garry Kasparov, who recovered to triumph in a six-game match in Philadelphia last year after the computer shocked the world by winning the first game.

"I know that at this point I'm not going to get a match with Kasparov on my own," Benjamin said, prompting laughter from the five computer scientists who are now his team-mates and daily companions at IBM's T.J. Watson Reserach Centre in Yorktown Heights.

"And I'm also well aware that this match is not me against Kasparov, but to be part of that kind of ultimate chess challenge is really the culmination of everything that I've worked for in my chess career."

Benjamin, 33, one of the strongest U.S.-born grandmasters playing on the international circuit, a former U.S. champion and regular member of the U.S. Olympiad team, describes his time on the Deep Blue team as "the experience of my life."

His involvement stemmed from twice winning the Harvard Cup -- a tournament pitting grandmasters against other chess-playing computer programmes -- and private testing with Deep Blue, an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess.
WON"T FACE KASPAROV DIRECTLY

During the games, Benjamin will not actually face Kasparov across the board making Deep Blue's moves. That task will most likely be given to scientist Hsu Feng-Hsiung, dubbed "a poker face" for the way he wielded the pieces in the 1996 match.

"I think it's psychologically important for Kasparov that there be somebody sitting on the other side. It's very hard to play against no opponent," Benjamin said. "We have a natural psychological advantage. Our player doesn't experience fear or stress or get tired."

The scientists say Benjamin has helped them supplement the computer's ability to look at hundreds of millions of positions per second with a greater appreciation for strategy and the relative value of pieces in certain positions.

The IBM chess project began with the aim of discovering how chess can be used to understand computer science applications such as data mining, financial modelling techniques, airline scheduling and molecular dynamics. Chess playing is considered ideal for computers because the game involves a specific number of physical objects governed by simple, clearly defined rules.
When the computer plays Kasparov, its calculations and moves will be transmitted from its 32 processors through telephone lines to a video display unit next to its human operator.

Benjamin is the envy of many of his fellow professional players. He spends every working day in the presence of a very strong player -- Deep Blue -- preparing for a match against Kasparov, considered by most experts to be the best in the history of the ancient game.

He said grandmasters were split over whether they wanted Kasparov or Deep Blue to win the $1.1 million six-game match in Manhattan from May 3 to May 11: "Some are anti-computer and some are anti-Kasparov."

For Benjamin, life at one of the biggest corporations on the planet could not be more different from the chaotic and divided chess world, where brilliant players travel from tournament to tournament trying to grind out results for meagre prize money sometimes amounting to a few thousand or just hundreds of dollars.

"Probably the best thing for my chess is that I've developed very good work habits from putting in 40-hour work weeks on chess, Benjamin said in his sparsely furnished office containing a desk, computer terminal and wooden chess set.
WARFARE IN THE WORLD OF CHESS

The chess world has been divided, sometimes bitterly, since 1993 when world championship finalists Kasparov and Nigel Short of England broke away from the game's governing body -- the International Chess Federation, known by its French acronym FIDE -- to form the Professional Chess Association (PCA).

Kasparov won the match against Short and defended his PCA title successfully against Viswanathan Anand of India in New York in 1995. Meanwhile, Kasparov's arch-rival Anatoly Karpov remained with FIDE and won two championships under its auspices in 1993 and 1996.

Chess organisers failed in their attempts to "re-unify" the crown by having Kasparov and Karpov play a match. FIDE announced this month that it had designed a new format for its world championship, a tournament of 100 players between Dec. 16, 1997 and Jan. 8, 1998 in Elista, capital of the former Soviet republic of Kalmykia.
Both men have been invited to compete, starting at the semi-final stage. They have not yet responded.

The political disputes in chess aside, Kasparov is still considered the world's best player. He has emphasised his superiority in recent months by winning two prestigious tournaments against his most formidable human challengers, including Karpov.
